title: 2  Cross-Validation: Student Exploration 1.2
text:
3 Thoughts from before class 09/01:
’’’To be honest, I really struggled reading this paper. I chose Cross-Validation: What Does It Estimate and How Well Does It Do It? by Bates et al. (2023). As a person who does not have a traditional stats or data science background, a lot of the topics were really unfamiliar to me. Initially, I used Copilot to compare/contrast a few of the vocab words (cross-validation, prediction error, data splitting, etc.), but I also had to consult Wikipedia quite often for exact definitions of many stats concepts. I found it much more beneficial to look at Wikipedia than to prompt Copilot because Wikipedia allows you to click on other topics from one page, and that helped me understand how the concepts were related. I think it would be most helpful to see examples of how traditional/naive cross-validation performs worse than nested cross-validation, but this paper did not really provide that other than a few diagrams which did not tell me much about how nested cross-validation could be used in the real world.
What I learned/thought was interesting from this paper: 1. Traditional cross-validation is not good at estimating the accuracy of model fit on observed training data, but it is good at estimating average prediction error across (sometimes unseen) training sets. 2. Folds must be disjoint for cross-validation to work. 3. The confidence intervals of traditional cross-validation are much too narrow (they do not encompass the outliers well). 4. The estimate of variance with traditional cross-validation is too small.
What I did not understand: 1. Where do the unseen training sets come from? 2. How is data splitting different from cross-validation? Does it depend on the number of folds? 3. Why is leave-one-out resampling empirical? What does empirical mean in this case? 4. What is asymptotic normality? 5. Can you cross-validate the cross-validation? 6. If you use cross-validation on a small sample size, do outliers have more impact? How can we use cross-validation on small sample sizes better?
I would like to explore the last question for my simulation. I would like to test traditional and nested cross-validation on sets of things I understand in the real world (perhaps on Charlottesville weather data because I think I could find that easily) and see if I can predict the weather from the last few days. I will find out whether traditional or nested cross-validation predicts it better and I will use a small sample size (maybe only the data from a month ago).’’’

title: 4  Module 3 GLM
text:
This is my analysis and computational exploration of Module 3’s Generalized Linear Models (Nelder and Wedderburn, 1972).

5 Concepts from this paper:

linear model: continuous outcome variable y with independent variables x subscript n where n is the number of independent variables

\(E[y|x1, x2, x3] = b0 + (b1x1 + b2x1^2 + b3x1^3)x3 + (b4x2 + b5x2^2 + b6x2^3)x3\), etc.
= b0 + {x3 = never, sum of i = 1-3 of }
mean E, variance V, OLS or MLE can estimate model (what is the best choice based on the data we have?)

generalized linear models (GLM): model we can fit when we assume the outcome is binary, Bernoulli, Poisson, binomial, etc. (logistic regression is an example); linear models generalized to distributions that are in the exponential family
probit analysis: assigning each variable a score based on how similar/close it is to the mean (z-scores? variance?)
density function:
logistic regression:
least squares: fitting line/curve/model/function to data (regression) by finding the residuals (true value - predicted value) of each point, then squaring the residuals (so they are positive), and adding them all up to find the total error; we want to minimize the total error to find the line of best fit (optimization)
weighted least squares:
distributions:

normal distribution: bell curve (continuous)
binomial distribution: bar chart where the x-axis is the number of positive outcomes and the y-axis is the probability of that number of positive outcomes, using multiple trials (discrete)
multinomial distribution:
Bernoulli distribution: one trial with two outcomes (discrete)
Poisson distribution: probability of events occuring in one (fixed) interval (discrete)
gamma distribution: includes the chi-squared distribution and other continuous probability distributions (continuous)


Parts of a GLM: - random component: how is the variable distributed? (normal, binary, Bernoulli, Poisson, binomial, etc.) GLMs allow this to be from the exponential family. - systematic component: linear combination of predictors (independent variables); looks like linear regression because it is of the form b0 + b1x1 + b2x2 + … + bnxn - link function: a function that connects the linear predictor to the expected value in the dataset


6 Expressing GLMs mathematically:
Usually we would express linear models as y = mx + b or some other equation that assumes all our data can fit a certain line or one of the distributions defined above. We use the same linear structure for the systematic component of GLMs: p = b0 + b1x1 + b2x2 + … + bnxn. I chose p to mean linear predictor. The b’s are the coefficients and the x’s are the variables. In linear regression, these variables would have to all be independent, but that is not necessarily the case for GLMs.


7 Demonstrating the model with code:
I used a dataset I found on Kaggle about animal shelter intakes and outcomes. I want to plot the probability of certain shelter outcomes based on the age upon outcome.


8 Visualizations of the prediction relationship:


9 Special considerations for using GLMs:
GLMs are good for data that is not linear (cannot be modeled well with linear regression). It is important to consider what your data is describing before choosing a model.
